title: IP Subnetting & CIDR: The Field Handbook
summary: A complete study-notes series on IPv4 addressing with CIDR: how prefix lengths carve address space, how to compute network, broadcast, and usable host ranges, how to split and aggregate subnets, which ranges are private or special, and how routers pick a route by longest prefix match.

chapters.title: Anatomy of an IPv4 Address
points: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit unsigned integer, written as four dotted decimal octets, e.g. 192.168.10.37 = 0xC0A80A25 = 3232238117
Each octet holds 8 bits, range 0-255; any octet above 255 makes the address invalid (256.1.1.1 is not an address)
Total IPv4 space = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 addresses, the root cause of exhaustion and of NAT's existence
Bit weights inside one octet: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 — memorize these, all subnet math falls out of them
An address alone is meaningless for routing; an address always carries an implied or explicit prefix length (an interface has 10.0.0.5/24, not just 10.0.0.5)
Every address splits into a network portion (leftmost bits, shared by all hosts on the link) and a host portion (rightmost bits, unique per host)
The split point is chosen by the network designer, not by the address itself — this is the whole idea of classless addressing
Terminology: prefix = network portion; host bits = the remainder; the pair (address, prefix length) is a 'prefix' or 'route' when it names a block

chapters.title: From Classful to CIDR
points: Classful addressing (pre-1993) fixed the split by the leading bits: Class A 0xxx = /8, Class B 10xx = /16, Class C 110x = /24
Class sizes were catastrophically coarse: a Class A gives 16,777,214 hosts, a Class C gives 254 — a site needing 500 hosts had to burn a whole Class B
Two crises drove the change: address exhaustion (wasted Class B space) and routing table explosion (thousands of un-aggregatable Class C routes)
CIDR (RFC 4632, originally RFC 1519, 1993) removed classes: the prefix length is carried explicitly, any length 0-32 is legal
CIDR notation: A.B.C.D/n where n = number of leading network bits, e.g. 172.16.8.0/22
CIDR enabled variable length subnet masking (VLSM) — different subnets of the same organization can have different prefix lengths
CIDR enabled supernetting/aggregation — 4 adjacent /24s advertised as one /22, shrinking global routing tables
'Classful' habits still leak into tools: some routers default an unmasked route to its classful length, and old exam questions assume /24 for 192.x — always state the prefix
Modern rule: class letters are historical vocabulary only; never let them determine a mask

chapters.title: Prefix Length and the Subnet Mask
points: A subnet mask is 32 bits: contiguous 1s for the network portion, then contiguous 0s for hosts — /24 = 255.255.255.0
Prefix length n and dotted mask are the same information in two notations; /26 = 255.255.255.192
Mask must be contiguous — 255.255.0.255 is not a legal mask on modern stacks (non-contiguous masks are dead)
Wildcard mask = 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask; /26 mask 255.255.255.192 has wildcard 0.0.0.63 (used in ACLs and OSPF)
Host bits h = 32 - n; block size (addresses in the subnet) = 2^h
Longer prefix = more network bits = smaller subnet = fewer hosts. /25 is half the size of /24, not double — the classic reversal mistake
The 'magic number' shortcut: increment = 256 - (mask octet value); for /26 increment is 64, so networks start at .0 .64 .128 .192
AND the address with the mask to get the network; the mask is literally a bitwise filter, not a separate database

chapters.title: Network Address, Broadcast, and Usable Range
points: Network (subnet) address = all host bits set to 0; it names the block and appears in routing tables
Broadcast address = all host bits set to 1; a packet to it reaches every host on that link
Usable host range = everything strictly between network and broadcast
Usable hosts = 2^h - 2 (subtract network and broadcast); /24 gives 254, /26 gives 62, /30 gives 2
Compute network by bitwise AND: 192.168.10.37 AND 255.255.255.192 = 192.168.10.0
Compute broadcast by bitwise OR with the wildcard: 192.168.10.0 OR 0.0.0.63 = 192.168.10.63
Worked example /26 on 192.168.10.37: network 192.168.10.0, broadcast .63, usable .1-.62, next subnet starts .64
Worked example /20 on 172.16.135.9: increment 16 in the third octet, network 172.16.128.0, broadcast 172.16.143.255, 4094 usable hosts
/31 (RFC 3021) is special: 2 addresses, both usable, no network/broadcast — designed for point-to-point links
/32 is a single host route, used for loopbacks, host routes, and BGP next-hops
Directed broadcast to a remote subnet's broadcast address is normally dropped by routers (Smurf-attack mitigation)

chapters.title: Subnetting Mechanics: Borrowing Bits
points: Subnetting = borrowing bits from the host portion and giving them to the network portion
Borrow b bits and you create 2^b subnets, each with 2^(h-b) addresses
Split 10.0.0.0/8 into 256 /16s, or into 65,536 /24s — the same arithmetic scales at any prefix
Sizing rule: to fit H hosts you need h host bits where 2^h - 2 >= H; 100 hosts needs h=7 (/25), because 2^6-2 = 62 is too small
Always size up to the next power of two — there is no /24.5; asking for 300 hosts costs you a /23 (510 usable)
VLSM: allocate largest subnets first, then carve smaller ones from the remaining space, to avoid stranding blocks
Subnet blocks must be aligned: a /26 can only start at an address that is a multiple of 64 in its octet — 192.168.1.100/26 is a host, not a network
The valid-subnet check: address AND mask must equal the address itself for it to be a network address

chapters.title: Aggregation and Supernetting
points: Aggregation (supernetting) is subnetting run backwards: merge adjacent blocks by shortening the prefix
Two blocks are aggregatable only if they are adjacent AND the combined block is aligned — 192.168.0.0/24 + 192.168.1.0/24 = 192.168.0.0/23, valid
Counter-example: 192.168.1.0/24 + 192.168.2.0/24 cannot become a /23; the /23 containing .1.0 is 192.168.0.0/23, so the merge would swallow .0.0 and miss .3.0
Method: write the candidate networks in binary, find the number of common leading bits, that count is the aggregate prefix length
Aggregation is why ISPs allocate on power-of-two boundaries — it keeps the global BGP table from exploding
Over-aggregation risk: advertising a /14 when you only own three of the four /16s black-holes traffic for the fourth
The default route 0.0.0.0/0 is the ultimate aggregate — zero network bits, matches every destination
Numbering tip: design address plans hierarchically (region -> site -> VLAN) so aggregation is possible later; flat random allocation can never be summarized

chapters.title: Private, Reserved, and Special-Use Ranges
points: 172.16.0.0/12 spans 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 — 172.32.x.x is public, a very common misread
Private addresses are not globally routable; ISPs drop them, so they need NAT to reach the internet
Loopback 127.0.0.0/8 — the whole /8, not just 127.0.0.1
Link-local 169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA): a host with this address failed to get DHCP
Carrier-grade NAT 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598) — looks private but is distinct from RFC 1918; used between subscriber and ISP NAT
Documentation ranges (RFC 5737): 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 — use these in write-ups, never a real customer's IP
Benchmarking 198.18.0.0/15, IETF protocol assignments 192.0.0.0/24, 6to4 relay anycast 192.88.99.0/24
Multicast 224.0.0.0/4, reserved/experimental 240.0.0.0/4, 'this network' 0.0.0.0/8, limited broadcast 255.255.255.255
Choosing 10.0.0.0/8 everywhere causes VPN/merger collisions; picking an odd /16 inside it (e.g. 10.147.0.0/16) reduces overlap pain

chapters.title: Routing Tables and Longest Prefix Match
points: A routing table entry maps a destination prefix to a next-hop and outgoing interface
Longest prefix match (LPM): among all entries whose prefix contains the destination, the router forwards using the one with the most network bits
LPM is the specificity rule — it is decided before administrative distance or metric; a /32 from a lowly static route beats a /24 from OSPF
Worked lookup for 10.1.2.7 against entries 0.0.0.0/0, 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16, 10.1.2.0/24: all four match, the /24 wins
The default route 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything and therefore always loses to any other match — it is the fallback by construction, not by priority
A /32 host route is the most specific possible match and overrides everything for that single address
LPM makes 'punching a hole' possible: advertise 10.0.0.0/8 to a datacenter but route 10.1.2.0/24 out a different link
The match test itself: destination AND entry_mask == entry_network
Order of table entries does not matter for routing (unlike ACLs and firewall rules, which are first-match, top-down) — confusing the two is a classic error
If no entry matches and there is no default route, the packet is dropped and ICMP destination unreachable (net unreachable) is returned

chapters.title: How Routers Actually Do the Lookup
points: Naive lookup = scan every entry, keep the longest match: O(N) per packet, unusable at ~1M BGP routes and line rate
Binary trie (radix tree): one node per bit, walk the destination bits from the left, remember the deepest node carrying a route — O(W) with W=32
Patricia/path-compressed trie collapses single-child chains, cutting memory and node visits — the classic BSD kernel routing structure
Multibit tries stride several bits per level (e.g. 8-8-8-8 or 16-8-8) to cut memory accesses at the cost of prefix expansion
LC-tries and LPC-tries add level compression for dense regions; Linux uses an LC-trie in fib_trie for IPv4
TCAM does LPM in a single clock cycle: entries stored with don't-care bits, sorted longest-first, hardware picks the first hit — fast but power-hungry and expensive per entry
Complexity summary row: linear scan O(N) time / O(N) space; binary trie O(32) / O(N*32); multibit trie O(32/k) / larger; TCAM O(1) / costly hardware
FIB vs RIB: the RIB is the full control-plane database (all protocols' routes); the FIB is the compiled forwarding structure the data plane actually reads
Route caching (flow-cache) was abandoned on backbone gear because cache-miss floods and DoS traffic destroy hit rates; full FIB lookup every packet is the norm
Prefix count growth is the real cost driver: a router's usable life is often ended by TCAM/FIB size limits, not by throughput

chapters.title: Practical Usage: Reading and Building Address Plans
points: Linux inspection: `ip -4 addr show` prints 'inet 10.0.5.23/24'; `ip route get 8.8.8.8` shows exactly which entry LPM selected
`ip route show` lists prefixes with scope and next-hop; the `default via ...` line is the 0.0.0.0/0 entry
`ipcalc 192.168.10.37/26` prints network, broadcast, host range, and host count — use it to check hand math, not to replace it
Python one-liner: `import ipaddress; n=ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.10.0/26'); n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses, list(n.hosts())[:3]`
Splitting in Python: `list(ipaddress.ip_network('10.0.0.0/22').subnets(new_prefix=24))` gives the four /24s
Membership test: `ipaddress.ip_address('10.1.2.7') in ipaddress.ip_network('10.1.0.0/16')` -> True
Cloud practice: AWS VPC CIDR must be /16-/28, and AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast) so a /28 gives 11 usable, not 14
Kubernetes gives each node a pod CIDR (often a /24 out of a cluster /16), which caps pods per node — a sizing decision made at cluster creation
Firewall/ACL rules are written as prefixes; `10.0.0.0/8` in a rule means the same bitwise test as a route lookup
Plan for growth: allocate the block you will need in 3 years, since renumbering a live network is far more expensive than reserving space

chapters.title: Comparisons and Trade-offs
points: Fixed-length subnetting vs VLSM: fixed is simpler to document and automate, VLSM wastes far less space — VLSM wins on any address-constrained network
/30 vs /31 on point-to-point links: /30 burns 4 addresses for 2 usable, /31 burns 2 for 2, saving 50% across thousands of links; /30 is more universally supported
Few large subnets vs many small subnets: large means bigger broadcast domains and noisier ARP; small means more routes, more gateways, more config
NAT vs public addressing: NAT conserves addresses and hides topology, but breaks end-to-end reachability, complicates inbound services, and adds state to the path
IPv4 + CIDR vs IPv6: IPv6 has 128 bits, no broadcast address, no address scarcity, /64 per link by convention — subnetting math becomes about hierarchy, not conservation
Aggregation vs specificity trade-off: aggregating shrinks tables but hides failures; deaggregating gives precise control but bloats the global table
Static routes vs dynamic protocols: statics are predictable and cheap, dynamic protocols react to failure but consume CPU/memory and need design discipline
TCAM vs software trie: TCAM gives deterministic single-cycle lookup at high power and cost; tries are cheap and scalable but variable-latency
Bigger prefix on the WAN vs more specific advertisement: providers may filter anything longer than /24 in BGP, so a /27 advertisement will simply be ignored on the internet

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Off-by-one on usable hosts: forgetting the -2, or subtracting 2 on a /31 where both addresses are usable
Assigning the network or broadcast address to a host — the interface may accept it but traffic behaves strangely or is silently dropped
Misaligned subnet: writing 192.168.1.100/26 as a network when the real network is 192.168.1.64/26
Believing /25 is larger than /24 — longer prefix means smaller block
Mask mismatch between hosts on the same link: 10.0.0.5/24 and 10.0.0.6/25 can ARP asymmetrically and appear to work in one direction only
Overlapping subnets in a plan (10.0.0.0/23 and 10.0.1.0/24) — LPM will still route, but address assignment collides and troubleshooting becomes brutal
Assuming 172.16.0.0/16 is the whole private Class B range; it is /12, covering 172.16 through 172.31
Treating routing tables like ACLs: routes are longest-match (order-free), ACLs are first-match (order-critical)
Overlapping RFC 1918 space between two sites joined by a VPN — requires renumbering or double NAT
Advertising an aggregate you do not fully own, black-holing the parts you do not host
Forgetting cloud-reserved addresses (AWS 5 per subnet, Azure 5) when sizing a small subnet
Ignoring the gateway: every usable subnet loses one more address to the router interface, so a /29 gives 6 usable but only 5 for hosts

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet and Recap
points: Core formulas: host bits h = 32 - n; block size = 2^h; usable hosts = 2^h - 2; subnets from borrowing b bits = 2^b
Magic number = 256 - mask octet; subnets start at multiples of the magic number
Network = address AND mask; broadcast = network OR wildcard; wildcard = 255.255.255.255 - mask
Private ranges to memorize: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16; plus 127/8 loopback, 169.254/16 link-local, 100.64/10 CGNAT
Routing rule: longest prefix wins, always; 0.0.0.0/0 is the last resort; /32 beats everything
Lookup cost: linear O(N), trie O(32), TCAM O(1) — production gear uses tries in software and TCAM in hardware
Design order: count hosts per segment, round up to a power of two, allocate largest first (VLSM), keep blocks aligned so they can aggregate later
Five-second sanity check on any subnet you are handed: is the network address a multiple of the block size? If not, the notation is wrong
Next steps: practice by converting an octet to binary daily, and read RFC 4632 (CIDR) and RFC 1918 (private space) end to end
